summary: This standards-track document addresses a reverse path forwarding check failure that can arise in TRILL active-active access when using the pseudo-nickname mechanism of RFC 7781. It resolves the issue using centralized replication of broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast traffic.

eli5.summary: When one announcement must reach everyone, a single helper makes the copies instead of many. This avoids confusion about where the announcement came from.

subtitle: Fixes dropped broadcast and multicast frames in TRILL active-active access by replicating them at one central node.

tldr.problem: With pseudo-nicknames for active-active access, broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast (BUM) frames can reach a transit RBridge on unexpected ports and be wrongly dropped by the Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) check.
tldr.mechanism: Edge RBridges send BUM traffic in unicast TRILL encapsulation to a centralized distribution tree root, which decapsulates it and sends it down its own tree. Transit RBridges compute the RPF check as if the centralized node were the ingress.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 6325 and adds two Nickname Flags bits, R and C. Centralized nodes and edge RBridges typically need software and hardware upgrades; transit RBridges typically need only software.

facts.label: Centralized node
facts.value: Must be a distribution tree root

today: RFC 8361 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6325. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The RPF Check Problem in Active-Active TRILL
sections.content:
TRILL (RFC 6325) provides loop-free, per-hop multipath forwarding with little configuration. It uses IS-IS as its control plane. Customer Equipment (CE) can be attached to several edge RBridges at once, called active-active access, so traffic is shared across all uplinks.

The pseudo-nickname mechanism of RFC 7781 stops MAC addresses from appearing to flip-flop on remote RBridges. A virtual RBridge with one pseudo-nickname stands for the whole edge group, and every member uses that nickname as the ingress nickname.

The catch is for BUM traffic. Transit RBridges between the ingress and the distribution tree root treat the traffic as coming from the virtual RBridge. If different edge RBridges of the same group use the same tree, frames may arrive at a transit RBridge on different ports. The RPF check then fails and the frames are dropped incorrectly.

This RFC updates RFC 6325. Normally multi-destination traffic is ingressed as a multi-destination TRILL packet. With centralized replication it is first ingressed as a unicast TRILL packet.
sections.eli5: If several doors on a building all say the same name, guards inside get suspicious when the same visitor shows up from different sides and turn them away. This fix avoids that.

sections.title: Centralized Replication Overview
sections.content:
An edge RBridge that gets BUM traffic from a CE sends it in unicast TRILL encapsulation to a centralized node, which MUST be a distribution tree root. Roots are normally high-capacity core RBridges, which makes it practical to support this with only software changes to transit RBridges.

In the TRILL header the ingress nickname is the pseudo-nickname when the frame came from an active-active port. The egress nickname is a special nickname of the centralized node called an R-nickname. An RBridge can hold several nicknames, so the node simply takes another one.

When the node receives a packet addressed to its R-nickname, it decapsulates it and replicates it down a distribution tree whose root is that node. The ingress nickname stays the same, so MAC learning at egress RBridges binds to the pseudo-nickname.

The RPF change is small. The RFC 6325 check tests a triple of ingress nickname, tree and receiving port. If the ingress nickname is marked as using centralized replication (a C-nickname), the check is based on distribution from the tree root. Otherwise it is based on distribution from the RBridge that holds the ingress nickname.
sections.eli5: Instead of every kid handing out invitations, they all give them to one teacher, who hands them out to the whole class. The teacher's spot is the one place everyone expects invitations to come from.

sections.title: A Worked Forwarding Example
sections.content:
The RFC's Figure 1 has RB5 as the distribution tree root and centralized node. CE1 and CE2 are active-active attached to RB1, RB2 and RB3, and CE3 is single-homed to RB3. The group uses the pseudo-nickname P-nick, and RB5's R-nickname is S-nick.

For BUM traffic from CE1 to CE2 and CE3: the ingress RBridge sends the traffic to RB5 in unicast encapsulation with ingress P-nick and egress S-nick. RB5 decapsulates it and sends it as a multi-destination packet on its own tree, with egress nickname nick5 and ingress still P-nick. RB4 receives it on the port facing the root, which passes the RPF check under the changed algorithm, and forwards it to RB1, RB2 and RB3.

Because P-nick matches the local active-active links to CE1 and CE2, those RBridges do not forward to CE1 and CE2, avoiding duplicates. RB3 forwards only to the single-homed CE3.
sections.eli5: The message goes to the central teacher, who sends it to everyone. Anyone who already got it directly from the sender ignores the second copy.

sections.title: Duplicates, Local Forwarding and Loops
sections.content:
To stop a CE receiving several copies from remote RBridges, the Designated Forwarder (DF) mechanism of RFC 7781 lets only one port of one RBridge per VLAN egress BUM traffic toward the edge group. Access ports are non-group, group DF or group non-DF.

The ingress RBridge uses local forwarding behavior A: replicate to group ports with the same pseudo-nickname as the incoming port, not to group ports with other pseudo-nicknames, and not to non-edge-group ports. If the ingress RBridge is itself the centralized node, behavior B applies: replicate to ports with the same pseudo-nickname, to DF ports with different pseudo-nicknames, and to non-edge-group ports, but not to non-DF ports with different pseudo-nicknames.

To avoid loops among RBridges in an edge group, a split-horizon check uses the ingress nickname to see whether an egress port belongs to the same active-active group as the incoming port. If two CEs use different ingress nicknames, their access ports should be isolated from each other so a CE does not get two copies.
sections.eli5: The first stop passes the message on locally only to the right neighbors. The rule is simple: do not send a copy back to where it came from, and do not send two copies to the same person.

sections.title: Load-Balancing Across Centralized Nodes
sections.content:
Several centralized nodes can share the BUM load by data label (VLAN or Fine-Grained Label). A node that should receive more traffic can hold two or more R-nicknames, and its share is proportional to how many it holds.

With k R-nicknames in the campus, the ingress RBridge orders them as unsigned 16-bit integers, numbers them 0 to k-1, and for data label ID m picks the R-nickname at index (m mod k) as the egress nickname.
sections.eli5: With several teachers, kids are split up by a number, like their class ID, so each teacher gets a fair share of the invitations.

sections.title: Coexisting with CMT and Upgrading
sections.content:
Centralized replication and the Coordinated Multicast Trees (CMT) solution of RFC 7783 both use pseudo-nicknames. They can coexist in one campus, and each edge group chooses independently.

An edge group using centralized replication MUST announce its pseudo-nickname with the C flag set in the Nickname Flags APPsub-TLV. A CMT group MUST NOT set the C flag, and a pseudo-nickname MUST NOT be shared between a centralized replication group and a CMT group. Otherwise BUM traffic could be pruned early and reach few or none of its targets.

For upgrades, centralized nodes typically need software and hardware changes, edge RBridges in active-active groups typically need software and hardware changes to do unicast encapsulation of BUM traffic, and transit nodes typically need only a software upgrade for the changed RPF calculation.
sections.eli5: Two different ways to pass out invitations can live in the same school, as long as each group clearly says which way it uses and they do not mix up their labels.

sections.title: The R and C Flags
sections.content:
Two new flags, R and C, are added to the Nickname Flags APPsub-TLV of RFC 7780. A nickname with R set is an R-nickname, held by a centralized node and used as the egress nickname for injecting BUM traffic. A nickname with C set is a C-nickname, used as the ingress nickname, and tells transit RBridges to use the special RPF algorithm.

If the advertising RBridge does not hold the nickname, the R and C bits are treated as zero. If an RBridge that is not a tree root advertises an R-nickname, it is treated as an ordinary nickname. If link-state information is inconsistent for a nickname, it is RECOMMENDED to treat the R or C flag as set if any Nickname Flags APPsub-TLV for it sets it.
sections.eli5: Two new stickers on a name tag: one says this is the central teacher, and the other says use the special checking rule for this name.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no extra security risks. A rogue RBridge that is a tree root could attract traffic by advertising an R-nickname, but it could already cause problems in other ways, such as advertising low-cost adjacencies. The protection is IS-IS authentication (RFC 5310) with the key given only to trusted RBridges.

IANA has assigned bit 2 (R, Replication Nickname) and bit 3 (C, Special RPF Check) in the NickFlags Bits subregistry.
sections.eli5: A fake teacher could try to collect the invitations, but a fake could already cause trouble in other ways. The answer is to give the secret key only to trusted teachers.
